limitations_and_boundaries: The study uses 2D scratch-wound and micropatterned assays, which may not fully recapitulate 3D tumor microenvironment.
Compressive stress level (5.8 mmHg) is an estimate from native breast tumor microenvironment; actual in vivo stresses may vary.
Shear forces during compression were calculated to be negligible (max 3.2 × 10−5 dyn/cm2), but other mechanical artifacts cannot be entirely excluded.
The role of E-cadherin was not necessary for compression-induced migration in 67NR cells, but other cell lines may differ.
The study focuses on a limited set of breast cancer cell lines; generalizability to other cancer types is unknown.
Long-term effects of compression beyond 16 h were not investigated.
The molecular mechanism linking compression to fibronectin secretion remains unidentified.
The selected source chunks do not report a rescue, reconstitution, reversal, or epistasis experiment; that rung of the causal evidence chain remains untested within this extraction scope.

research_questions.statement: Does mechanical compressive stress affect tumor cell migration and invasion?

provenance.text_excerpt: compression can initiate directional protrusions for leader-cell formation independent of actomyosin contractility; however, the contractile machinery is still necessary for sheet migration.

claims.statement: Compression-induced leader cell formation is independent of actomyosin contractility, but actomyosin contractility is required for sheet migration.

experiments_or_tasks: 67NR cells were treated with dominant-negative RhoA (RhoT19N), ROCK inhibitor Y-27632, MLCK inhibitor ML-7, or myosin II inhibitor Blebbistatin, and subjected to compression (5.8 mmHg) for 16 h. Leader cell formation and wound closure were assessed.

methods.name: Pharmacological and molecular inhibition of actomyosin contractility
methods.protocol_description: Cells were transduced with dominant-negative RhoA retrovirus or treated with Y-27632 (5 or 30 μM), ML-7 (25 μM), or Blebbistatin (50 μM) to inhibit actomyosin contractility.

study_units.name: Role of actomyosin contractility in leader cell formation and migration

experiments_or_tasks: 67NR cells were patterned into circles, rosettes, and squares using microcontact printing to control free-cell perimeter, and cultured under stress-free or compressed (5.8 mmHg) conditions. Leader cell formation and migration were analyzed.

methods.name: Microcontact printing
methods.protocol_description: Cells were seeded on surfaces stamped with fibronectin to form circles, squares, and rosettes, controlling free-cell perimeter.

study_units.name: Leader cell formation and free-cell perimeter

claims.statement: Compression enhances cell-substrate adhesion through localized secretion of fibronectin, not transcriptional upregulation.

experiments_or_tasks: 67NR cells were compressed (5.8 mmHg, 16 h) or left uncompressed. Cell-substrate adhesion was measured by resistance to fluid shear detachment. Fibronectin distribution was assessed by immunofluorescence, and fibronectin mRNA was measured by qPCR. Cycloheximide treatment was used to inhibit protein synthesis.

methods.name: Cell adhesion assay
methods.protocol_description: Cells were exposed to detractive fluid shear, and remaining adherent cells were quantified by crystal violet staining (OD 540 nm).

methods.name: Immunofluorescence and qPCR
methods.protocol_description: Fibronectin and vinculin were stained and imaged by confocal microscopy; fibronectin mRNA was measured by quantitative real-time PCR.

experiments_or_tasks: Five mammary epithelial cell lines (MCF10A, MCF7, 67NR, 4T1, MDA-MB-231) were subjected to constant compressive stress (5.8 mmHg) for 16 h using a weighted piston device, and migration was measured via scratch-wound assay.

methods.name: In vitro compression device
methods.protocol_description: Cells were pressed against a membrane surface with a weighted piston to apply defined compressive stress (5.8 mmHg) for 16 h.

methods.name: Scratch-wound assay
methods.protocol_description: Migration rates were measured by imaging the denuded area over time after scratching the cell monolayer.
